name: Proto-Punk
editorial_article: Proto-punk refers to the diverse, scattered, and unpolished rock music that emerged during the 1960s and early 1970s, long before the term "punk rock" existed as a defined movement or subculture. It is a retrospective label used by critics and historians to categorize artists who anticipated the raw energy, aggressive attitude, and simplistic structures that would eventually define the punk explosion of 1976 and 1977. Because proto-punk was never a cohesive or centrally organized movement, its roots are deeply heterogeneous, drawing from mid-1960s garage rock, the theatrical sensibilities of glam rock, and the rough-and-tumble pub rock scene in the United Kingdom. \n\nMusically, proto-punk acts were often united by a defiant, "do-it-yourself" sensibility. They were generally out of step with the prevailing counterculture of the era, opting for stripped-down, primitive production and visceral, often confrontational performance styles. The center of gravity for American proto-punk was largely in Detroit, where bands like The Stooges and MC5 pushed the garage rock aesthetic to its logical, chaotic conclusion. Meanwhile, in the underground scenes of New York, Cleveland, and Ohio, artists were experimenting with similarly jarring, minimalist sounds. In Britain, the precursors to punk often emerged under the banners of glam or pub rock, emphasizing a return to the basics of rock and roll. Ultimately, proto-punk serves as the vital link between the early, high-energy R&B-influenced rock of the 1950s and the ideological intensity of the punk movement that followed.
editorial_definition: A retrospective term for the raw, unconventional rock music of the 1960s and early 1970s that prefigured the themes, aesthetics, and sound of the punk rock movement.
